Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Well, it's getting more and more painful to fill up at a gas station or fill a tank of oil to heat your home. And we all know why.

Look, we're making progress shifting to other sources of energy to heat our homes, but we're still the most dependent on heating oil to heat our homes in the in the entire country. That reliance on heating oil makes us vulnerable to great shifts in global energy markets that drive up costs for Maine people and businesses. This president's war in Iran right now has created the largest fuel supply disruption in global history and has driven energy prices to record highs. The price of heating oil in Maine has reached more than $6 a gallon, so you'll be paying almost $800 more to fill a standard 275 gallon tank than you did a year ago. Kerosene prices are also reaching historic highs, all because of this war.

Maine people should not be forced to choose between staying warm or putting food on the table because the president chose to drag us into a needless war -- and an endless war, it appears.

My administration is doing what it can to help people save money on heating costs and stay comfortable in their homes this winter.

It's not enough, but I've directed the Department of Health and Human Services to identify households that would be eligible for $40 million in discounts on their electric bills through Maine's Low Income Assistance Program, or LIAP. Starting in November, thousands of eligible families who are customers of CMP or Versant will begin to see discounts ranging from 20 percent to 80 percent, and these will be applied automatically every month to their electric bills. It's one thing we can do. Families who already get federal assistance for home heating oil through LIHEAP, the Low Income Energy Assistance Program, will also be enrolled automatically in this state assistance program, LIAP, to get the maximum savings on their electric bills without any unnecessary paperwork. Customers with questions about this discount should contact their electric company directly.

I've also called on Congress to increase funding for federal home heating assistance, and I thank Maine's congressional delegation for their bipartisan support for LIHEAP funding, despite the president's attempts to eliminate this program. And that's just not enough, though, to make up for the skyrocketing costs driven by tariffs and the president's war. Congress must ensure the safety and comfort of Maine people heading into this winter season by increasing LIHEAP funding.

In the meantime, MaineHousing has distributed about $4 million to heating fuel companies for some of our most vulnerable households, those with older adults on small incomes or small children. Those trucks will begin delivering fuel to those homes over the next few days. We're also talking to farmers and foresters and other entities that use diesel fuel a lot about other ways we might be able to help them address high diesel prices here in Maine.

I'm proud to say that thanks to our investments over the years in energy efficiency and clean energy, our reliance on heating oil has fallen from 70 percent of Maine households in 2010 to just over 50 percent now. Still, it's not enough. My administration will continue to make it as affordable as possible to transition to clean energy sources like heat pumps, to save people money, and to make sure we're not left to shoulder the burden of the president's blunders.

Are you interested in exploring heat pumps or using wood or propane to heat your home instead of oil and kerosene? Are you curious about energy assistance programs? Weatherization? Do you need contact information for local community action agencies or MaineHousing or Efficiency Maine Trust? Our Winter Heating Guide, published every year by the Maine Department of Energy Resources, has all that information, as well as some helpful tips about winterizing and saving money, and about contact information, and links to online resources. You can view and download that Winter Heating Guide and review the latest heating fuel prices at Maine.gov/Energy.

This crisis affects all of us – low income, middle income, everyone who has a home, everyone who has a bill to pay this winter. But as the weather continues to get colder, I encourage all Maine people to see how they might save money and stay warm through the winter by using our current Maine Winter heating guide found at Maine.gov/Energy.

This is Governor Janet Mills. Please stay warm, and thank you for listening.

Sonderling was officially sworn into office Oct. 2. “It is the honor of my life to serve as the 31st Secretary of Labor and continue my service to the Department under President Trump’s leadership,” said Sonderling. “I believe President Trump is the greatest President for the American worker and job creator. My mission is to ensure that American workers have the skills and resources they need to seize the incredible job opportunities being created across the country thanks to the tireless work of this Administration.” Upon announcing his nomination, President Trump said, “Throughout his career, Keith has proven his dedication to delivering strong results for the Hardworking People of our Country, and I know he will do an incredible job in his new role.” While serving as Deputy Secretary of Labor, Sonderling oversaw the department’s day-to-day operations, including strategic planning, budget formulation, financial management, information technology, and human resources. From September 2020 to August 2024, Sonderling served as a Commissioner of the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, including as Vice Chair from 2020 to 2021. During his tenure, he became a leading global voice on super intelligence in the workplace, publishing extensively and speaking around the world on SI and the future of work. Following his service at the EEOC, Sonderling led President Trump’s Department of Labor transition team before returning to the Department in January 2025. During President Trump’s first term, Sonderling served as Acting Administrator, Deputy Administrator, and Senior Policy Advisor of the department’s Wage and Hour Division from 2017 to 2020. In June 2026, President Trump designated Sonderling as Acting Director of the U.S. Office of Government Ethics, a position he continues to hold concurrently with his service at the Department of Labor. During President Trump’s second term, Sonderling has also served as Acting Director of the Institute of Museum and Library Services and Acting Under Secretary of Commerce for Minority Business Development. Before entering government service, Sonderling was a partner at Gunster, one of Florida’s oldest and largest law firms, where he practiced labor and employment law.

When Region 6 courts transition to eFiling on December 7, they will be the second-to-last judicial region to implement eFiling. Earlier this year, courts in Judicial Regions 2, 7, 8, 1, and 4 made the switch from paper filing to eFiling. The Maine Judicial Branch remains on track to have all courts on the new system by February 2027.

Supreme Judicial Court Chief Justice Valerie Stanfill noted, "We are pleased that the transition from paper filing to eFiling has proceeded so smoothly this year, a testament to the hard work and dedication of all Judicial Branch staff. The eCourts project implementation and project support teams have traveled all over the state to make the transition successful, and they certainly deserve special acknowledgement."

Attorneys, government agencies (except law enforcement agencies), and parties who file more than six non-emergency cases in a calendar year, are required to eFile in courts that have implemented Maine eCourts. Self-represented parties are not required to eFile and can continue to file documents as they always have, in paper at the courthouse, by mail, or by email if filing a protection from abuse or harassment case.

Maine eCourts is a suite of applications and web-based tools provided by Tyler Technologies' Enterprise Justice Software. The system allows for the management of court dockets and hearings, storage of digital case files, eFiling, and online payments.

MaineCare Coverage of Gender-Affirming Care for Medicaid Beneficiaries Under Age 18 and Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Enrollees Under Age 19

Oct 09, 2026

As described in the message sent September 18, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) published a final rule in the Federal Register on August 13, 2026, that limits federal Medicaid and CHIP funding for certain gender-affirming care provided to minors. This rule prohibits federal matching funds for puberty blockers, cross-sex hormone therapy, and surgical interventions when used for gender transition for Medicaid beneficiaries under age 18 and CHIP enrollees under age 19. The federal rule is scheduled to take effect on October 13, 2026. 

The federal rule does not prohibit states from using state-only funds to cover these services. Maine law requires MaineCare to cover medically necessary treatment for or related to gender dysphoria and protects members from discrimination based on gender identity or gender expression.   

To ensure we are in compliance with this new federal rule, we have established the billing requirements below for providers who deliver gender-affirming care services to Medicaid beneficiaries under age 18 and CHIP enrollees under age 19. 

Effective on October 13, 2026, medical claims submitted through the MIHMS system must: 

  • Include applicable gender-affirming care diagnosis codes on all claims. 
  • Include the SE modifier on any claims submitted for gender-affirming care, other than behavioral health services.  
    • The SE modifier is used to identify a service that must be reimbursed using state-only funds.  
    • The SE modifier should be listed after any other modifiers on the applicable claim line(s). 
    • Behavioral health treatment for gender dysphoria is still eligible for federal match, so providers are not required to include the SE modifier on behavioral health-related claims.  

Effective on October 9, 2026, pharmacy claims submitted through the MEPOPS system must:  

  • Have Prior Authorization (PA) as required on the Department’s Preferred Drug List. This requirement applies to preferred and non-preferred products on the Department’s identified medication list.   
  • Include the medication’s intended clinical use by including the applicable diagnosis code and the information needed to determine the appropriate coverage and funding pathway.  
    • Medication prescribed for a clinical use outside the scope of 42 CFR § 441.801–441.802 and 457.476 remains subject to the otherwise applicable MaineCare pharmacy criteria. For medication prescribed for use within the scope of those provisions, the Department will review coverage under its separately funded state-only benefit.  

This PA requirement is used to determine clinical purpose and payment source. It does not, by itself, change the drug’s preferred status, establish additional step therapy, or mean that all uses of the medication are excluded from federally matched coverage. Existing drug-specific clinical criteria continue to apply as appropriate.  

For questions, please contact Provider Relations Specialist, Lisa Bouchard.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Contact: Danna Hayes

Danna.hayes@maine.gov

If You Bought Certain Generic Prescription Drugs in the United States Between May 2009 and December 2019, You Could be Eligible for Money

AUGUSTA – Attorney General Aaron M. Frey today joined a coalition of 45 states and territories seeking court approval of three settlements with Ascend Laboratories, Citron Pharma and Mayne Pharma to resolve allegations that the generic drug manufacturers engaged in a widespread, long-running conspiracy to artificially inflate and manipulate prices, reduce competition, and unreasonably restrain trade with regard to numerous generic prescription drugs.

Ascend will pay $400,000 to the states. Mayne will pay $650,000. Citron’s settlement only includes non-monetary terms as it has ceased business operations. As part of the settlement, the companies each agreed to meaningful injunctive terms including a series of internal reforms to ensure fair competition and compliance with antitrust laws. 

These latest settlements come as the States prepare for the first trial to be held in Hartford, Connecticut in February 2027.  

The States previously reached settlements with Sandoz, Glenmark, Lannett, Bausch, Apotex, Heritage, and Heritage’s parent company, Emcure, totaling $496.5 million.

If you purchased a generic prescription drug between May 2009 and December 2019, you may be eligible for compensation. To determine your eligibility, call 1-866-290-0182 (Toll-Free), email info@AGGenericDrugs.com or visit www.AGGenericDrugs.com. You can submit a claim for compensation.

Connecticut is leading a coalition of nearly all states and territories engaged in a series of antitrust cases, starting first in 2016. The first Complaint included Heritage and 17 other corporate Defendants, two individual Defendants, and 15 generic drugs. Two former executives from Heritage Pharmaceuticals, Jeffery Glazer and Jason Malek, have since entered into settlement agreements and are cooperating. The second Complaint was filed in 2019 against Teva Pharmaceuticals and 21 of the nation’s largest generic drug manufacturers. The Complaint names 16 individual senior executive Defendants. The third complaint, to be tried first, focuses on 80 topical generic drugs that account for billions of dollars of sales in the United States and names 26 corporate defendants and 10 individual defendants. The States filed a fourth complaint earlier this year, alleging that Novartis AG, Sandoz Group AG and Sandoz AG, are liable for Sandoz’s alleged conduct and for fraudulently transferring assets.

The cases all stem from a series of investigations built on evidence from several cooperating witnesses at the core of the different conspiracies, a massive document database of more than 20 million documents, and a phone records database containing millions of call detail records and contact information for more than 600 sales and pricing individuals in the generics industry. Each complaint addresses a different set of drugs and defendants and lays out an interconnected web of competing industry executives that met with each other during industry dinners, "girls’ nights out," lunches, cocktail parties, golf outings, and communicated via frequent telephone calls, emails, and text messages that sowed the seeds for their illegal agreements. Throughout the complaints, defendants use terms like "fair share," "playing nice in the sandbox," and "responsible competitor" to describe how they unlawfully discouraged competition, raised prices, and enforced an ingrained culture of collusion. Among the records obtained by the States is a two-volume notebook containing the contemporaneous notes of one of the States’ cooperators that memorialized his discussions during phone calls with competitors and internal company meetings over a period of several years.

States and territories also joining the settlements include: Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.

MaineCare in Education: Updated Joint Individual Education Program (IEP) Guidance for School Health-Related Services

Oct 08, 2026

As a reminder, all providers who deliver services following the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) must ensure all MaineCare-covered services are documented following the Department of Health and Human Services/Maine Department of Education Joint IEP Guidance document. 

The Maine Department of Education has released updated Joint IEP Guidance to help schools follow federal and state requirements. The updated guidance was developed through a collaborative effort and is available on the MaineCare in Education web page. 

DOE first released the Joint Guidance on August 28, 2026, and has re-issued this guidance effective September 18, 2026. The reissued guidance replaces the previously issued Joint Guidance and provides clarification in response to questions and feedback received from School Administrative Units (SAUs), providers, and other interested parties. 

All IEP documents must reflect the updated guidance as soon as possible, but no later than thirty (30) days of the issuance of the guidance. 

Providers with current prior authorizations for School Health-Related Services through Acentra should upload any updated documentation to Atrezzo. Acentra will accept IEP language from both versions through October 18, 2026. Beginning October 19, 2026, Acentra will only accept IEP language from the new version re-issued on September 18, 2026. 

For technical assistance regarding the billing and processing of MaineCare claims, please contact your Provider Relations Specialist. 

For all other questions related to the provision of MaineCare School Health-Related Services, please contact Trista Collins, State Medicaid Educational Liaison.    

For technical information related to IEP development, please contact Dan Hemdal at the Maine Department of Education.

 [¶1]  Jerome Weiss appeals from a decision of a Workers’ Compensation 
Board administrative law judge ( Smith, ALJ) denying his Petition to Reopen for 
Mistake of Fact or Fraud. Mr. Weiss contends that the ALJ erred in determining that 
his petition was untimely under 39-A M.R.S.A. § 321(2), and in concluding that even

Company committed fraud. We disagree with Mr. Weiss’s contentions and affirm the 
decision. 
 
 
2 
 
I.  BACKGROUND1 
 [¶2]  Mr. Weiss sustained a work-related shoulder injury on February 3, 2009, 
while working for Maine Soapstone  Company. Initially, Maine Soapstone 
voluntarily paid Mr. Weiss lost time and medical benefits. On September 13, 2010, 
Maine Soapstone issued a 21-day letter informing Mr. Weiss and the board of their 
intention to discontinue Mr. Weiss’s benefits as of October 5, 2010. See 39-A 
M.R.S.A. § 205(9).

a Petition for Review , Request for Provisional Order , and a Petition for Award of 
Compensation regarding the February 3, 2009, date of injury. During the litigation, 
Mr. Weiss underwent an independent medical examination with Dr. Hall. See 39-A 
M.R.S.A. § 312. Dr. Hall opined that the effects of Mr. Weiss’s injury were ongoing 
and that he had retained a partial work capacity. An evidentiary hearing was held on 
May 16, 2011, before a board hearing officer (Pelletier, HO).2

items.title: US Department of Labor cites Pennsylvania excavation employer for failing to provide trench protection following fatal trench cave-in — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: CHAMBERSBURG, PA – The U.S. Department of Labor has cited an excavation contractor for willful and serious safety violations after a young worker was fatally injured in a trench collapse. The department’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration opened an investigation into Jonas David Wagoner – doing business as J.D. Wagoner Excavating – on April 2, 2026, and found workers were installing a storm sewer system 12 feet below ground level in a trench that was not adequately protected from soil collapse. When a portion of the trench's wall failed, the unrestrained soil engulfed one worker. The agency issued a willful violation for failure to protect workers from cave-ins and two repeat violations for failing to assign a competent person to conduct daily trench inspections and removing employees from hazardous conditions.In addition, the employer received three serious violations for failure to provide construction hazard prevention training to employees, establish a safe means for workers to exit the excavation site, keep materials at least two feet from the edge of an excavation site, and restrain side materials from becoming roll-in hazards.   OSHA proposed $254,884 in penalties. The employer has 15 business days from receiving receipt of its citations and penalties to request an informal conference with OSHA’s area director or contest the findings before the independent Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission. Please check the OSHA establishment search page periodically for any changes in the inspection or penalty status.Visit OSHA’s website to learn about keeping workers safe around trenching and excavations. Employers can also contact the agency for information about OSHA’s compliance assistance resources and for free help on complying with OSHA standards.

items.title: Energy Conservation Program: Test Procedures for Commercial Warm Air Furnaces — Federal Register — Documents Matching 'Maine'
items.content_text: The Department of Energy ("DOE" or "the Department") is withdrawing the test procedure for commercial warm air furnaces adopted under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, specifically appendix B, "Uniform Test Method for Measurement of the Energy Efficiency of Commercial Warm Air Furnaces (Thermal Efficiency Two)." Upon reconsideration, DOE has determined that appendix B would have an uncertain increase in representativeness that does not outweigh the likely increase in burden. DOE has also determined that withdrawing the appendix B test procedure would be consistent with the proposed Process Rule, which states that for certain categories of equipment, including CWAFs, DOE will adopt the industry test procedure, as contemplated by EPCA, except in very limited circumstances. Commercial warm air furnaces will continue to be subject to the testing requirements of appendix A, "Uniform Test Method for Measurement of the Energy Efficiency of Commercial Warm Air Furnaces (Thermal Efficiency)."

What is the process for tabulating ranked-choice ballots? (PDF)

Ranked choice voting results tabulation glossary

This glossary explains the terms used in the ranked-choice voting results grid that is produced to explain the results of any ranked-choice race. See our Election Results page.

Round 1

This is the first round of ranked-choice voting tabulation, which begins to apply the RCV rules onto the ballots that were cast on Election Day. (Note: The unofficial Election Day tally can be considered as Round 0). For example, if a voter did not mark any candidate as their first choice, their ballot was counted as blank on election night. In Round 1, if the voter marked the ballot for their second choice candidate, their vote is bumped up and counted, per the RCV rules.) Rounds continue until only two candidates remain and the winner is determined as the candidate with more than 50% of the votes in that final round.

Exhausted ballot

There are no valid votes in any ranking on the voter’s ballot for any continuing candidate (a candidate who is still in the race and has not been defeated). Types of exhausted ballots:

  • Exhausted choices: For those ballots that are exhausted by exhausted choices, all of the voter’s candidate choices have been eliminated from the race. (Note: If they cast a vote for a candidate who has been eliminated, their vote remains with that candidate, just as it would in a plurality race if they had voted for the losing candidate.)
  • Undervote: The voter did not mark any candidates, or refrained from ranking, in that choice category (1st, 2nd, 3rd). Those whose ballots are exhausted by undervote either didn’t vote in this race at all, or they left BOTH their first and second choices blank (in which case, we do not look any further down their ballot, per the RCV rules).
  • Overvote: The voter chose more than one candidate for that ranking. For example, the voter marked BOTH Candidate A and Candidate B as their choice.

Continuing ballots

All ballots that include a valid vote for a continuing candidate, and therefore have not been exhausted.

Transfer

The votes that go to a continuing candidate when another candidate is eliminated. This is determined by reviewing each ballot initially cast for the eliminated candidate. The elections software looks further down each voter’s ballot to see if the voter ranked another candidate who is still in the race, and if so, it moves or “transfers” their vote to that candidate (For example: Your vote transfers to your second choice candidate if your first choice candidate is eliminated from the race).

Total=

Ballot Exhausted by Overvotes + Ballot Exhausted by Undervotes + Exhausted Ballot + Continuing Ballots.

Maine Senate Confirms Vaughan Woodruff as Chair of the State Workforce Development Board

October 5, 2026

For Immediate Release

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA - The Maine Senate confirmed Vaughan Woodruff, principal of EquinoxDG, to a second term as chair of the State Workforce Development Board (SWDB). Gov. Janet Mills announced her nomination of Woodruff on Sept. 8, 2026. Woodruff has served as chair of the SWDB since 2023.

Prior to founding EquinoxDG, Woodruff was vice president of regulatory reform at the Interstate Renewable Energy Council and vice president of workforce development and interconnection strategy at ReVision Energy, where he oversaw the company's long-term strategic vision for training and talent development and developed nationally recognized registered apprenticeships in clean energy.

"The State Workforce Development Board plays a critical role in coordinating Maine's workforce development efforts to support economic growth and address workforce challenges," said Maine Department of Labor Commissioner Laura Fortman. "Vaughan Woodruff is a well-respected business leader with deep workforce expertise. His continued leadership will help maintain momentum as we strengthen Maine's workforce and economy."

"I appreciate the trust that Gov. Mills and the Maine Senate have placed in me through my nomination and confirmation to continue serving the people of Maine in this role," said Woodruff. "I feel privileged to work with the outstanding staff and members of the Board to increase the accessibility of the workforce system to Maine workers and businesses and to proactively address the workforce challenges ahead of us."

Woodruff is a seventh-generation Maine native who was raised in Pittsfield. He earned a bachelor's degree in civil engineering from the University of Maine and a master's degree in education from Prescott College in Arizona. Woodruff was the founder and CEO of Insource Renewables, an employee-owned solar company that was recognized as a Best for the World for Workers company by B Lab prior to its acquisition by ReVision Energy in 2021.

During Woodruff's tenure as chair, the SWDB has:

  • Launched Work Source Maine, the state's online resource connecting job seekers, students, parents, educators, career counselors and employers with resources to explore, plan and achieve career and workforce goals;

  • Launched the Maine Workforce Pell program, which expands federal Pell Grant eligibility to approved short-term, career-focused training programs that deliver industry-recognized credentials and measurable employment results, preparing students for in-demand occupations; and

  • Secured $15M+ in funding to support industry partnerships in advanced manufacturing, forest bioproducts and defense, and expand career exploration, job supports, and upskilling investments including registered pre-apprenticeships

As chair, Woodruff will continue to work with the SWDB, state agencies, education and training providers, employers and other partners to strengthen Maine's workforce development system and help connect Maine people with career opportunities.

Woodruff serves on the Electrical Technologies Advisory Committee at Kennebec Valley Community College and previously served on the Western Mountains Committee of the Maine Community Foundation and the Pittsfield Planning Board. Woodruff lives in Pittsfield with his wife, Holly Zadra, and their two sons, Eamon and Goran.

In person absentee voting – Maine’s version of early voting – is part of the special sauce that makes voting convenient to the citizenry and drives up turnout,” said Secretary Bellows. “Anyone can vote early for any reason starting today until October 29, and there are lots of ways to vote absentee – in person, by mail or utilizing a secure ballot drop box.”

This week, voters who are not able to make it to the polls on Election Day or who simply wish to avoid the crowds can begin casting absentee ballots, either in-person at their local town hall or by mailing back their signed and sealed ballot or dropping it in a local secure ballot box. As absentee voting gets underway, Secretary Bellows urged voters to make a plan to ensure their ballots are returned by close of polls on Election Day. “It’s exciting – Election Day will be here before we know it, and now is the time to make your voting plan,” she said.

Oct 05, 2026

Reminds Maine people and visitors ticks remain active even as temperatures fall

As days get shorter and leaves begin to change, ticks remain active across Maine. The Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) urges all Maine people and visitors to protect themselves from tick bites this fall.

Ticks can be active throughout the fall and during winter days, whenever temperatures rise above freezing. Fall is a busy time for outdoor activities, bringing people into contact with ticks more often. People may encounter them during everyday fall activities, like cleaning the yard or hunting.

Current year preliminary counts from the Maine Tracking Network show that health care providers reported over 5,000 cases of tickborne disease so far this year. This includes diseases like Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, and babesiosis.

“Many people think ticks are only a summer problem, but ticks can remain active throughout the fall,” said Maine CDC Director Puthiery Va. “You can enjoy Maine’s beautiful fall weather and outdoor activities while staying safe by taking a few simple steps before, during, and after can help protect you from tickborne disease.”

Ticks often live in wooded and brushy areas and areas with leaf litter. The Maine CDC encourages everyone to think TICKS when spending time outdoors: 

  • T – Take an EPA-approved repellent and use it before going outside. Use DEET, picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon eucalyptus on skin. Pre-treat clothing with permethrin.
  • I – Inspect your body daily. Check yourself, children, and pets for ticks after spending time outdoors.
  • C – Cover your skin. Wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants and tuck pants into socks. Light-colored clothing makes ticks easier to spot.
  • K – Know your surroundings. Be aware when you are in tick habitat and take extra precautions.
  • S – Shower after being outdoors. Showering helps wash off ticks before they attach. Put clothes in the dryer on high heat for at least 15 minutes before washing to kill ticks.

Remember to check for ticks after any outdoor activity and before bed each night. Check in areas where ticks may be easy to miss, including the scalp, behind the ears, under the arms, around the waist, between the legs, and behind the knees.

The most common symptoms of tickborne disease include flu-like symptoms. People who have Lyme disease may also find an expanding rash somewhere on their body. This rash can sometimes, though not always, look like a bullseye. If you experience any of these symptoms, talk to a health care provider and be sure to mention any recent tick exposure.

The University of Maine Cooperative Extension Tick Lab offers tick identification for free and tick testing to Maine residents for a $20 fee. Testing can take up to three days and should be used for surveillance purposes only, not for diagnosis. Finding a tick on you, even if it was attached, does not necessarily mean that it spread any germs to you. Find more information at ticks.umaine.edu. 

To learn more about how to stay tick free, visit the Maine CDC's website.

October Is National Disability Employment Awareness Month

October 1, 2026

Gov. Janet T. Mills has proclaimed October 2026 as National Disability Employment Awareness Month (NDEAM).

Maine is an Employment First state, affirming employment as the first and preferred option for people with disabilities who receive services from state agencies. The governor's proclamation calls on employers, schools, higher education institutions and community organizations to promote access to good, in-demand jobs and career pathways, including registered apprenticeship.

Get involved this October!

This year marks the 81st anniversary of NDEAM, and organizations across Maine and nationally are offering events, trainings and other activities throughout the month. Whether you're an employer interested in inclusive hiring, a jobseeker exploring career opportunities, a workforce professional, a student, a family member or a community partner, there are ways to participate.

We encourage you to browse the events and activities below.

Thank you for helping celebrate the contributions of people with disabilities and promote access to meaningful employment and career opportunities across Maine.

To help promote awareness, printable MDOL NDEAM posters are also downloadable here. For more information about employment services for people with disabilities, visit the Maine Department of Labor's Bureau of Rehabilitation Services.

October NDEAM-related events and activities

For employers and workforce development professionals

- October: Every Wednesday this month, Global Best Buddies celebrates NDEAM during its #WorkplaceWednesday series will share video stories of employees, employers, and partnerships showing what inclusive employment looks like in action.

- Oct. 6: Part of the 2026 Latinos with Disabilities Community Series, Workplace Inclusion & Economic Opportunities for People with Disabilities webinar is hosted by United Cerebral Palsy and sponsored by ANCOR Foundation and Waymo. During this panel discussion from 3 to 4 p.m., disability advocates and Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) experts will explore employment rights, workplace inclusion, and reasonable accommodations.

- Oct. 13: This monthly online Maine Apprenticeship Information Session at 11 a.m. provides a brief overview of the Maine Apprenticeship Program and how it connects employers and individuals to earn-while-you-learn career pathways.

- Oct. 20: Navigating Performance Discussions and the Accommodation Process Effectively online training is offered through the Job Accommodation Network from 2 to 3 p.m.

Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave Program Publishes Actuarial Report, First Claims Report

October 1, 2026

For Immediate Release: Oct. 1, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

Actuarial report projects PFML Trust Fund will remain stable for the next 10 years

AUGUSTA - The Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML) program has published its second annual actuarial report, as well as its first claims report on Oct. 1, 2026.

PFML became law in 2023 and is a statewide program that provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of paid leave for medical, parental, family care, military family or safe leave.

The PFML program began accepting claims on March 30, 2026, and began paying benefits on May 1, 2026. This initial claims report covers the program's first three months of claims activity, from March 30 through June 30, 2026. Future claims reports will be published annually and will cover a full year of claims activity.

Highlights of the reports include:

  • The PFML Trust Fund remains solvent and based on updated revenue and claim expenditure, is projected to remain stable for the next 10 years.
  • The program received 8,376 applications between March 30 and June 30, 2026.
  • Among the claims approved, medical leave was the most common reason, followed by welcoming a new child and caring for a family member. Other leave reasons represented a very small portion of the overall claim volume.

"We are excited to see the PFML Program effectively off the ground and helping Maine workers and businesses through life's big moments, both now and for years to come," said PFML Director Luke Monahan.

More information on the PFML program, including how to apply, can be found on the program's website: https://www.maine.gov/paidleave/

Employees, employers and self-employed individuals with questions can call 207-621-5024 between8 a.m. and 5 p.m. Monday through Friday. Employees can send a message through the Benefits Application Portal, while employers and self-employed individuals can send a message through the Maine Paid Leave Contributions Portal.

items.title: Maine State Archives offers expanded digital access with Open Access — Maine Secretary of State — Bureau of Corporations, Elections & Commissions News
items.content_text:
AUGUSTA, MAINE
– Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today announced the official launch of Open Access, the Maine State Archives (MSA) new online platform for publicly accessible, digitized and born-digital public records. The platform can be accessed at
https://digitalarchives.maine.gov
or from the Maine State Archives section of the Secretary of State website.
Open Access is the public-facing side of a strategic effort to maintain a digital preservation system for records of Maine state government. The system ensures the long-term preservation and accessibility of state records that are archival or subject to long-term retention.
“From the beginning, I have been committed to improving efficiency and modernizing our systems to benefit Mainers and streamline access,” said
Secretary Bellows
. “Open Access will provide improved government transparency in a user-friendly platform that will be continuously expanded as more and more collections are imaged.”
Overall, MSA’s collections span five centuries from the 1639 royal land grant to Sir Ferdinand Gorges to the 2024 papers of the Lewiston Tragedy Commission. One section of the site is devoted to Maine history before statehood, highlighting important records such as Revolutionary War land grants and the Rolls and Rosters Book of Orders for the 8th Division of the Maine Militia. The records of Maine’s involvement in the Civil War are extensive. Open Access currently holds just over 100,000 imaged records so far.
“With more than 8 miles of documents in the Archives care, there is a long way to go to digitize them all, but it’s a great start,” said Maine State Archivist Christian Cotz. “We’re excited to continue to add records to the platform and provide Mainers from students to researchers with even more to discover each time they visit the site.”

items.title: US Department of Labor awards $10.2 million to 67 organizations to promote workplace safety and health training — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration today announced the award approximately $10.2 million in grant funds to 67 organizations across the nation to support education and training focused on worker safety to help employees and employers recognize serious workplace hazards and employ safety and health programs.Funded through the Susan Harwood Training Grant Program, the grants aim to advance worker safety and health by providing instructor-led training opportunities for workers and employers in small businesses with an emphasis on industries with high injury, illness, and fatality rates.The grants will fund training and education on hazard awareness, prevention, and controls to protect workers from on-the-job hazards through the development of quality classroom-ready training and educational materials that identify and prevent workplace hazards.The grants honor the legacy and work of Dr. Susan Harwood who, during her 17 years with OSHA, developed workplace safety guidelines for benzene, formaldehyde, bloodborne pathogens and lead in the construction industry. Harwood was also primary author of OSHA’s cotton dust standard which virtually eliminated byssinosis – a lung disease that causes asthma-like symptoms – among textile workers.Learn more about the Susan Harwood Training Grant Program and 2026 awardees.
